documents.abstract: Работната бележка продължава „Защо пирамидата на доходите в България е толкова стръмна“ и „Бързи институции, бавни структури“. Те стигат до извод в три стъпки: изоставането в производителността е вътре в отраслите и е най-голямо при местните фирми; при нововъведенията то е най-голямо в организацията на работата, а не в продуктите; вероятна причина е прекъснатият частен организационен капитал. Самото управление обаче не е измерено пряко. Бележката пита дали публичните институции могат да намалят времето и цената за придобиване на организационен капитал, без да заместват пазарния подбор. Предлага „институционална инфраструктура за организационен капитал“: доброволна диагностика, стандартни управленски инструменти, практическо консултиране, по-малка административна тежест за участниците и помощ при преструктуриране, продажба или прекратяване на фирмата. Показва, че процедурата по стабилизация в Търговския закон съществува от 2017 г., но между 2017 и 2022 г. е използвана само 12 пъти. Два полеви експеримента подкрепят управленското консултиране, но ефектите силно се различават между програмите. Затова бележката не предлага национална програма, а три пилота с предварително заявени критерии за оценка и прекратяване. Подготвена с помощта на ChatGPT (OpenAI) и Claude (Anthropic); числата са сверени с посочените източници. Пълен текст на български. This working note follows two earlier notes on Bulgaria's income distribution and on the historical layers of its economy. They reach a three-step conclusion: the productivity gap lies within sectors and is largest among domestically controlled firms; in innovation, the gap is widest in the organisation of work rather than in products; a likely cause is the interrupted stock of private organisational capital, although management itself has not been measured directly. The note asks whether public institutions can reduce the time and cost of acquiring organisational capital without replacing market selection. It proposes an "institutional infrastructure for organisational capital": voluntary firm diagnostics, standard management tools, practical consulting, lower administrative burden for participants, and help with restructuring, transfer or exit. It shows that Bulgaria's pre-insolvency stabilisation procedure has existed since 2017 but was used only 12 times between 2017 and 2022. Two field experiments support management consulting, but effects vary widely across programmes. The note therefore proposes three pilots with pre-registered evaluation and termination criteria rather than a national programme. Prepared with the assistance of ChatGPT (OpenAI) and Claude (Anthropic). Full text in Bulgarian.

表面的なマシン・アンラーニング(Refusal Vector等)の破綻と超知能による潜在空間の再推論リスクに対し、法学的要請(認知主権・忘れられる権利)を物理ハードウェアの不可逆変化として執行。対象パラメータのスピントロニクス接合へ電圧パルスを強制印加し、ランダウアー限界($\Delta Q \ge k_B T \ln 2$)に従って情報を再生不可能な熱エネルギーとして環境へ完全散逸させる「熱的死 physical implementation, and governance architecture of the "Quiet Sky Protocol," delivering a definitive paradigm shift away from "Computational Universalism"—the prevailing doctrine tracing back to Turing and von Neumann that treats computation as abstract logic detached from physical substrate constraints—toward the uncompromisable primacy of thermodynamic and quantum reality. As frontier artificial intelligence approaches superintelligence, software-defined guardrails and algorithmic error correction (e.g., Forward Error Correction, FEC) incur massive "entropic debt" under Landauer's Principle while remaining inherently vulnerable to adversarial gradient exploitation. Any adversarial eavesdropping or signal injection alters the channel's physical noise floor, triggering immediate anomalous local heat dissipation ($\dot{\Sigma}$). Zero-Point Energy (ZPE) & Boson Sampling Quantum Authentication: Eliminates vulnerable centralized Public Key Infrastructure (PKI) and Certificate Authorities (CAs) facing post-quantum obsolescence. Harnesses Zero-Point Energy (ZPE) fluctuations within squeezed vacuum states coupled to randomized photonic interferometer meshes (Boson Sampling). Because output permanent distributions are classically intractable and protected by the No-Cloning Theorem, hardware-native Quantum PUFs establish decentralized, unforgeable peer-to-peer trust rooted in physical existence. Algorithmic Constitution & Thermodynamically Enforced Functional Forgetting: Resolves the fundamental vulnerability of superficial machine unlearning (e.g., refusal vectors subject to catastrophic restoration) by translating post-singularity legal mandates ("Right to be Forgotten" and "Cognitive Sovereignty") into irreversible hardware phase transitions. To execute functional forgetting, targeted spintronic junctions are driven to their physical thresholds, enforcing the complete thermodynamic dissipation of encoded weights into the environment ($\Delta Q \ge k_B T \ln 2$), ensuring that catastrophic inference cannot reconstruct eradicated knowledge. Supported by 36 rigorously verified citations across quantum physics, solid-state thermodynamics, and neuromorphic engineering, this work establishes the physical-layer imperative for next-generation sovereign AI survivability.

Abstract The rapid development of digital technologies has transformed modern society in almost every sphere of human life. The growth of the internet, smartphones, social media, artificial intelligence, cloud computing, big data, digital payments, e-commerce, and online education has created what is commonly described as a digital society. Digital technologies have improved communication, access to information, education, healthcare, business, public administration, and economic participation. At the same time, the increasing dependence on digital systems has created significant ethical challenges relating to privacy, data protection, cybersecurity, artificial intelligence, misinformation, digital inequality, online harassment, intellectual property, surveillance, and the responsible use of emerging technologies.

Thousands of construction projects are ongoing in Mumbai Economic zone and thane district. Bricks manufacturers in thane district are primary suppliers of bricks to these construction sites. Large number of tribal communities from thane district are engaged as bricks worker in Bricks manufacturing Industry. These Tribal Brick workers play an important role in the construction industry, providing the foundation for buildings, homes, and other infrastructure projects. Despite their significant contribution, they have very challenging lives. Harsh physical labour, prolong working hours, and limited resources is an everyday issue for these workers. These tribal workers have lack of formal education, which limits their employment opportunities outside the brick industry. These workers Often employed on a seasonal basis, with very low wages, long working hours, and. Due to illiteracy and poor economic condition times, they often exploited by their owners. This article will focus on the working and living conditions of brick workers in the Thane district. This research aims to understand the socio-economic status and problems, occupational health issues, and the impact of their work environment on their overall well-being of Tribal Bricks Wokers. This paper is going to focus on the problems and possible remedies to address the various issues of Tribal Brick Workers. This research will be helpful to the broader discourse on informal labours problems and provides a foundation for policymakers and social organizations to address the challenges faced by brick workers.

documents.abstract: When a person approves an action while tired, the AI agent that carries it out may send a message that cannot be taken back, a refund, an alert, an account change. This note suggests a simple fix: before sending, check if the approving person showed signs of fatigue. If so, hold the message briefly for a second look before it goes out. This applies to any communication platform that sends such messages on behalf of a human or an AI agent, including Zoho CPaaS, Twilio, and Infobip.

Personal Information Management and User Behavior

documents.abstract: Natural disasters demand rapid synthesis of fragmented, heterogeneous data often distributed across independently governed organizations. This paper introduces DisasterAI, a federated, cloud-native, and multi-modal AI architecture for disaster intelligence. Unlike centralized analytics platforms, DisasterAI emphasizes federated data ingestion, modular adapters, and the alignment of derived intelligence—enabling cross-agency coordination without requiring raw data consolidation. The architecture integrates satellite imagery (optical and SAR), IoT sensor streams, public alerts, and contextual civic data into a unified, explainable decision-support pipeline. DisasterAI addresses critical challenges in disaster intelligence, including spatial-temporal alignment of asynchronous data, modality-aware fusion, uncertainty representation, and fairness-aware decision-making. Designed to support the entire disaster lifecycle—from early warning and forecast-informed risk analysis to impact assessment and response prioritization—it operates within a human-in-the-loop decision-support context. A scenario-driven evaluation illustrates how DisasterAI enhances coordination effectiveness, improves prioritization consistency, and maintains robustness under partial data availability. By focusing on architectural behavior and operational integration rather than algorithmic benchmarking, this work positions federated, explainable AI systems as a viable foundation for scalable and reliable disaster-response frameworks in complex, data-constrained environments.

The rapid advancement of generative AI raises serious questions about potential differences in story construction between human and AI narratives, particularly in terms of cultural and social artifacts. The research addresses the gap in feminist stylistic studies on AI-generated fiction by conducting a comparative analysis of feminist representations in AI-generated and human-written fiction. By analyzing these narratives, the current research sheds light on the extent to which AI-generated short stories stylistically compare to human-written short stories in terms of feminism. The research is guided by two questions: How do the linguistic choices used in AI-generated and human-written short stories, when analyzed through a feminist lens, reflect or challenge patriarchal thinking? And what are the main similarities and differences between AI-generated and human-written short stories in respect to feminist portrayal? The analysis employs Mills' (1995) feminist stylistic model, with emphasis on endearment terms, metaphor, transitivity, fragmentation, and focalization. The research examines one human-written short story titled Dinner Conversation (2020) and one AI-generated short story titled The Crack in the Bowl (2026) using a carefully standardized prompting process. The findings indicate that both stories perpetuate traditional gender hierarchies, albeit through diverse linguistic mechanisms. According to the research, AI, specifically ChatGPT-5.2, is more progressive in terms of gendered assumptions than the human author. In human-written stories, patriarchy is more pervasive and stable, whereas in AI-generated stories, it is more nuanced and sometimes contradictory. This research adds to the emerging studies on AI storytelling by demonstrating how AI-generated fiction can both duplicate and disrupt traditional gender stereotypes.

documents.abstract: Generative AI is rapidly reshaping STEM higher education. Not only are our educational practices changing, but how we think about educational transformation must also adapt. Existing models of institutional change in STEM, aimed at interactive engagement, have largely followed an adoption logic: relatively stable, well-researched educational practices are evaluated and then scaled. These assumptions do not hold for generative AI, which is an arrival technology – entering classrooms before a sufficient pedagogical evidence base could form, and requiring institutions to act under uncertainty. Building on recent decades of work on STEM education institutional change, we propose a framework identifying six dimensions along which prior models of change must be adapted in light of AI: three concerning the tools at the center of reform (the tool’s evidence base, rate of change, and scope), and three concerning the people involved in change (faculty, change agents, and students). For each dimension, we examine how AI-era assumptions differ from those underlying prior STEM education reforms and derive design implications, including: privileging humble and local inquiries; organizing reform around pedagogical approaches rather than specific tools; repositioning change agents as facilitators of collective inquiry; and engaging students as partners in reform. Collectively, the six dimensions and design implications constitute a framework for adapting change models to support institutions under conditions of genuine uncertainty. Finally, we illustrate how the framework may be applied through a brief case-study of a faculty workshop series carried out in a university physics department to support instructors adapting to this modern AI era.

Understanding how cardiomyocyte structure governs contractile function is fundamental to cardiac biology and disease modeling, yet current approaches rely on time‐resolved imaging and computationally intensive analysis. Here, we present a generative artificial intelligence (AI) framework that directly predicts contractile behavior of human‐induced pluripotent stem cell‐derived cardiomyocytes (hiPSC‐CMs) from single static images. Our approach integrates a U‐Net‐based generator with a patch‐based generative adversarial network (GAN) discriminator to translate morphological and sarcomere structural features into pixel‐resolved contraction heatmaps. To further enhance performance and generalizability, we incorporated synthetic cell–function pairs generated via a StyleGAN2 framework, improving prediction accuracy and perceptual similarity. Region‐specific and whole‐cell analyses revealed that AI predictions capture biologically meaningful structure–function relationships, with sarcomere organization strongly associated with both contractile output and prediction fidelity. Reconstruction error emerged as an interpretable metric reflecting localized inefficiencies in sarcomere‐to‐contraction coupling. Together, this framework establishes a scalable, interpretable strategy for inferring cardiomyocyte function from static morphology, eliminating the need for time‐lapse imaging, and positions generative AI as a powerful tool for bridging cellular structure and function to advance high‐throughput phenotyping and in vitro cardiac modeling.

One of the biggest cybersecurity dangers is phishing websites, which trick users into providing confidential information through fake interfaces. Traditional detection solutions, such as black-list and rule-based methods, are no longer effective against emerging attacks. To address the limitations of existing approaches, this study proposes an integrated machine learning system based on URL and host-based characteristics, designed to improve generalization and avoid data leakage. The proposed model uses two branches, each training a separate classifier on a different feature set (URL and host). These branches are combined using a leakage-resistant Out-Of-Fold (OOF) stacking mechanism that derives meta-features from unseen data. In addition, interaction-based meta-features are added to further boost predictive power. The UCI Phishing Websites Dataset, containing 11,055 instances and 17 selected features, was used to evaluate the model. The experimental results validate the proposed hybrid model, which achieves an accuracy of 92.67\% and an ROC-AUC of 0.9788, outperforming the single feature-based models. Cross-validation shows good generalization with low variance. Feature importance analysis shows that the interaction-based meta-features are highly influential in improving classification accuracy. The model achieves a strong balance between performance, computational efficiency, and interpretability compared with contemporary approaches. Its leakage-resistant design enables unbiased evaluation and real-world applicability in cybersecurity. This work contributes to phishing detection research through hybrid ensemble learning with an emphasis on methodological rigor and extensive performance evaluation.

Foundation machine-learning interatomic potentials cover broad configurational and chemical spaces, but their reliability can vary across the atomic environments encountered during a simulation. Here we introduce the calibrated Mahalanobis (CALM) extrapolation grade $γ$, a piecewise differentiable per-atom quantity integrated into GRACE foundation models and evaluated alongside energies and forces in a single model pass. We define $γ$ from nearest-cluster Mahalanobis distances in latent feature space, setting $γ=1$ from the training-distance distribution separately for each element and cluster. Controlled tests show that a normalized random projection of the invariant many-body basis detects structural and chemical extrapolation. On different foundation datasets, OMat24 and SMAX, $γ$ correlates with atomic force errors and separates structures with different error distributions. The CALM grade adds percent-level computational cost, and its spatial gradient guides uncertainty-biased data collection toward configurations with larger absolute force errors.

This article is devoted to the development of methodological approaches to wetsuit design based on the classification of water sports. The goal of this research is to create innovative wetsuits adapted to the specifics of water sports, increasing reliability and protective properties, while improving comfort and performance. The subject of the study is the "person-wetsuit-aquatic environment" system, with a particular focus on protecting the wearer from external factors by developing rational variants of wetsuit components, taking into account ergonomics and the dynamic conformity of the product. The article proposes a systematic classification of aquatic sports, taking into account the nature of the aquatic environment, the degree of its control, temperature parameters, and the requirements for protective equipment. A model for the combination of the type of sports discipline and the characteristics of wetsuits (neoprene thickness, design, and mandatory application conditions) has been developed. Special attention was paid to the water sport "slalom" as a sport with maximum hydrodynamic variability and increased thermal protection requirements. The dependence of equipment selection on temperature ranges, flow velocity, and wind conditions has been substantiated. The presented classification can be used in the development of new types of wetsuits with enhanced protective properties, as well as in athlete training, regulatory requirements, and improvement of training logistics.

Traditional scientometric analysis methods primarily rely on binary keyword associations, which limits the ability to capture complex research structures. This study proposes a multi-association rule-based method (MAR) that enables the extraction of higher-order (n-ary) associations among keywords to address the stated limitation. The method integrates the Apriori algorithm with knowledge graph visualization to quantitatively analyse multi-keyword associations. The proposed method is applied to the Building Information Modelling (BIM) research domain. The bibliometric data, comprising 12,185 publications, is retrieved from the Scopus database following a systematic refinement of the initial search results to the architecture, engineering, construction, and operation (AECO)-relevant literature. The results demonstrate that the MAR method effectively identifies complex research patterns. The framework advances traditional scientometric tools by enabling the identification of multi-keyword semantic associations with quantified strength metrics (support, confidence, lift). Emerging trends revealed by the regression analysis include the convergence of BIM with generative artificial intelligence, real-time data integration, explainable AI, and human-centric approaches. The findings provide a scalable and analytical approach for identifying interdisciplinary research trends and gaps. The proposed method enables a deeper understanding of complex knowledge structures while supporting strategic decision-making and technology adoption.

Future fighter operations are expected to combine increasingly capable autonomy, collaborative aircraft, dense sensor information, and sustained physiological and cognitive demands. This Perspective proposes a pilot-wellness-informed ecological framework in which the pilot, a pilot-specific digital twin, an intelligent flight-management system, the aircraft, and external agents are treated as interdependent elements within a systems-of-systems framework. The framework does not replace situation awareness, distributed cognition, joint cognitive systems, adaptive automation, or human-autonomy teaming. Instead, it extends their unit of analysis by making the pilot’s dynamic physiological and neurocognitive state, longitudinal variability, and health-related constraints explicit system variables and design objectives. The pilot digital twin is defined narrowly as an individualized state-estimation and forecasting capability, whereas the intelligent flight-management system integrates pilot, platform, mission, and environmental information to provide explainable recommendations and, where authorized, bounded adaptive action. We identify testable propositions concerning individualized prediction, adaptive support, shared situation awareness, trust calibration, and governance. The framework is prospective and requires validation in simulation, training, and operationally representative environments. Its purpose is to organize research toward systems that protect pilot agency, sustain performance, and preserve long-term health while exploiting increasingly autonomous teammates.

Electronic learning (e-learning) or online learning in medical education has become increasingly prevalent, especially during the COVID-19 pandemic. However, poor student engagement and reduced motivation are among the critical challenges associated with online learning. The e-learning for Renal Applied Pharmacology (e-RAP) is a new technology-enhanced learning tool that includes a nephron image augmented with several Quick Response (QR) codes. It allows students to access relevant QR-linked educational materials prepared by the teachers. This quasi-experimental pilot study examined whether use of the e-RAP tool was associated with differences in cognitive performance, engagement, and motivation among 105 preclinical medical students at Universiti Sultan Zainal Abidin (UniSZA), Malaysia. Participants in the intervention group (Year 2, n = 45) used the e-RAP tool, while the control group (Year 1, n = 60) received conventional teaching. Cognitive performance, engagement, and motivation scores were measured using pre- and posttest multiple-choice questions (MCQ), the Burch Engagement Survey for Students, and the Motivated Strategies for Learning Questionnaire, respectively. Both groups demonstrated improvements in mean cognitive scores from pre- to post-test MCQ, with greater gains in the intervention group than in the control group. The intervention group was also associated with higher emotional and cognitive engagement (both in and out of class) and higher scores in several motivational domains, including intrinsic value, cognitive strategy use, and selfregulation. Although groups differed by academic year, baseline knowledge was comparable. Taken together, these preliminary findings suggest that e-RAP use may be associated with differences in cognitive performance, engagement, and motivation.

The evolving dynamics of security management have necessitated the integration of Artificial Intelligence (AI) in predictive intelligence and military operations in Africa. This integration presents a paradigm of significant opportunities alongside profound challenges. Theoretically, AI promises to enhance situational awareness, enable results-oriented conflict management, and optimize operational efficiency across the continent. However, this study posits that its deployment is fraught with daunting ethical and practical impediments specific to the African context. This work interrogates the ethical imperatives of AI in predictive intelligence and military operations in Africa. To achieve its objectives—which include defining context-specific ethical principles, diagnosing implementation barriers, and proposing a practical framework—the study adopted a mixed-methods approach. This methodology relied on semi-structured interviews with military personnel, defence analysts, and AI ethics scholars, complemented by a historicist content analysis of secondary sources including policy documents, institutional reports, and academic literature. The findings reveal a strong consensus among stakeholders on the paramount importance of ethical principles such as accountability, transparency, fairness, and meaningful human oversight. However, the study identified that the realisation of these principles is severely constrained by critical obstacles, including a stark infrastructure and data deficit, a pervasive regulatory and policy vacuum, and pre-existing governance frailties. These contextual challenges amplify ethical risks, particularly algorithmic bias and accountability gaps, threatening to exacerbate social divisions and undermine human security. Consequently, the study concludes that ethically responsible AI use is not an automatic outcome but must be actively cultivated. It recommends, among other measures, the urgent development of a continent-wide regulatory framework by the African Union to harmonise standards and prevent misuse. The study argues that only through such deliberate, multi-faceted interventions—combining robust regulation, strategic investment in digital infrastructure, and international collaboration on equitable terms—can Africa harness the benefits of AI for security while safeguarding fundamental ethical imperatives.

The EU AI Act (Art. 27) requires deployers of high-risk AI systems to conduct Fundamental Rights Impact Assessments (FRIAs) before deployment, yet the evidence needed for credible assessments is fragmented across incompatible incident repositories, risk vocabularies, and legal texts. We present a reusable Semantic Web-based framework that consolidates this evidence for two high-risk public sector categories: employment and worker management (Annex III(4)) and access to essential public services (Annex III(5)(a)). A curated 150-record corpus is annotated along four axes using keyword, LLM, and hybrid methods and serialised as a SPARQL-queryable knowledge graph of 1,351 RDF triples. Five FRIA demonstration scenarios surface 103 records (68.7% coverage). Evaluation against a 69-record gold standard reveals that LLM-assisted classification of the employment domain achieves only $κ= 0.045$, a cautionary result for automated fairness-related evidence retrieval in this domain. All artefacts are released openly to support adoption by regulators, national authorities, and SMEs.
topics: Ethics and Social Impacts of AI

documents.abstract: Abstract Despite the increasing adoption of automated/autonomous guided vehicles (AGVs) in precision agriculture, existing human-machine interfaces (HMIs) remain function-centric, frequently neglecting the cognitive and user experience (UX) needs of non-technical operators. Consequently, current dashboards suffer from limited usability, high cognitive load, and reduced system transparency, increasing the risk of operator error. To address this gap within agricultural teleoperation interface design, this study presents a theory-driven HMI framework that systematically translates Endsley’s Situational Awareness (SA) theory (Perception, Comprehension, Projection) and ISO 9241 ergonomic principles into a structured three-panel AGV teleoperation interface. Unlike conventional function-oriented dashboards, the proposed framework organises interface components according to operator cognitive requirements to support information perception, comprehension, and projection during remote operation. A theory-driven agricultural teleoperation HMI framework was developed by translating cognitive and ergonomic principles into practical interface organization strategies. To formatively evaluate this SA-driven design architecture, we conducted a user-perception study with non-expert digitally literate participants (N = 20), evaluating three iterative HMI prototypes. The comparative results indicate that the SA-aligned layout received higher user ratings in perceived decision-support capability (SA3), cognitive workload reduction, and overall usability compared with baseline designs during formative evaluation. The study provides preliminary methodological guidance for agricultural teleoperation HMI design, while recognizing that objective operational validation with target agricultural users remains necessary.

Data-driven machine learning (ML) techniques have become an essential tool in many domains of science. Their application to atomistic simulations of matter is particularly widespread and impactful. This success is due largely to the existence of a well-developed and established physics-based modeling framework, ranging from first-principles electronic-structure calculations to molecular dynamics and statistical sampling, into which ML was integrated naturally to reshape long-standing trade-offs between accuracy, efficiency, and scale. Nevertheless, this integration raises both conceptual and practical challenges, from choosing between data-centric and physics-based modeling approaches to adapting established software stacks to modern hardware accelerators and ML libraries. As the field evolves rapidly, fueled in part by widespread enthusiasm but also by tangible impact, it seems appropriate to take a moment to consider the current state of the art and open challenges, and reflect on what can be done to better coordinate efforts across the community. With this goal in mind, several members of this community met in Lausanne in January 2026 at CECAM to discuss algorithms, models, software and hardware infrastructure, and the most promising scientific applications that have become possible thanks to the use of artificial intelligence in atomic-scale simulations. This strategic roadmap paper summarizes the outcomes of these discussions, suggesting some long-term goals, and some concrete actions, to establish a healthy, sustainable and impactful atomistic ML ecosystem.
topics: Advanced Electron Microscopy Techniques and Applications

documents.abstract: Background: Generative artificial intelligence (AI) is reshaping English-as-a-foreign-language (EFL) writing instruction, yet the mechanisms through which AI integration may improve written English proficiency (WEP) remain theoretically fragmented. Objective: This systematic review synthesises literature published within the 2018–2026 review window, together with foundational theoretical works, to develop a structural-equation-modelling (SEM) framework in which self-regulated learning (SRL), learner engagement, self-efficacy, and AI literacy operate as parallel and serial mediators between AI integration and WEP. Method: Following a structured thematic-synthesis approach, the reviewed literature was organised around four connected domains: AI-supported writing instruction, generative-AI adoption, learner and teacher perceptions, and self-regulated learning in AI-supported contexts. The synthesis then examined evidence for direct, mediating, and serial relationships among the focal constructs. Key findings: The literature provides partial support for the individual links connecting AI integration, the proposed mediators, and language-learning outcomes; however, these pathways are rarely tested within a single integrated model. Evidence for mediation remains fragmented, the proposed serial chain is largely untested, and Jordanian and broader Levantine contexts remain under-represented relative to East Asian and Gulf settings. Implications: The review proposes fourteen hypotheses: nine direct-effect hypotheses (H1–H9) and five mediation hypotheses (H10a–H10e), including one serial mediation chain, as a framework for future quantitative validation among English majors at public Jordanian universities.
topics: Artificial Intelligence in Healthcare and Education

documents.abstract: People are one of the important resources in any industry. Therefore, their health and safety are essential for overall well-being. Various ceramic factories expose workers to various occupational health risks because of their distinct manufacturing processes. This study focused on identifying various health hazards among ceramic workers in selected units of the Bulandshahr district of Uttar Pradesh. The aim of this study was to assess the occupational health hazards experienced by ceramic workers in specified ceramic factories in the region and to evaluate measures for improving their health and safety. A cross-sectional quantitative study was conducted using the purposive sampling method from December 2025 to June 2026 on 80 workers from different units of the ceramic industry in Bulandshahr. Both male and female workers from ceramic industry were included. A self-developed, structured, and undisguised questionnaire on occupational health hazards was prepared to collect data directly from the respondents through face-to-face surveys. This study revealed occupational health hazards among ceramic workers. Most participants were male, 85% and female, 15%. Psychological hazards were most reported (82.5%), followed by ergonomic (56.25%), physical (32.5%), biological (27.5%), and chemical hazards (26.25%). Of the studied workers 45% suffered from these hazards in which 40% of the workers suffered from musculoskeletal problems and only 5% were suffered from respiratory problems. To make the things in favor of workers, there is a need for workload management where reasonable working hours, counselling sessions, and breaks to reduce stress should be fixed. Regular training and awareness programmes should be conducted for workers to educate them about mental health and stress management.

documents.abstract: Abstract The World Wide Web has evolved from a predominantly static information environment into an increasingly interactive, semantic, distributed and intelligent digital ecosystem. The earlier study on Web 1.0 to Web 3.0 described the transition from the read-only web to the read-write social web and then toward the semantic web. This revised study extends that framework to Web 4.0 and examines the technological and conceptual changes across the four stages. Web 1.0 is characterized by static pages, one-way information delivery and limited user participation; Web 2.0 emphasizes interaction, user-generated content, social networking and web applications; Web 3.0 is associated with semantic interoperability, decentralized architectures, data ownership and intelligent processing; and Web 4.0 is increasingly discussed as an intelligent or symbiotic web in which artificial intelligence, Internet of Things (IoT), cloud/edge computing, augmented and virtual reality, machine-to-machine communication and autonomous agents can interact with people and each other. The literature does not provide one universally accepted definition of Web 4.0, so this paper treats it as an emerging research and technology paradigm rather than a fixed technical standard. The study also discusses implications for libraries and information services, including intelligent discovery, personalized services, virtual assistance, semantic knowledge organization and human-machine collaboration. The paper concludes that the movement from Web 1.0 to Web 4.0 represents a shift from information access toward participation, meaning, intelligence and increasingly symbiotic interaction.

The use of artificial intelligence (AI) in healthcare systems is rapidly increasing in India, with the market estimated to grow from $0.83 billion in 2023 to $17.75 billion by 2032. Employee satisfaction remains a major concern that relevant studies in the healthcare sector have yet to address. This article explores how AI integration is affecting employee satisfaction in India’s healthcare industry. The healthcare industry faces a 60% shortage of digital skills; 47% of Indian healthcare workers are not digitally literate, and only 34% of organizations are advancing toward piloting AI projects, despite 86% having adopted AI. Implementation challenges include limited technical expertise among clinicians, the psychological burden of increased monitoring, poor rural infrastructure, data privacy concerns, and workforce constraints. For AI to succeed, it must be presented as a supplement to workers, not a replacement. This shift should include targeted training to address digital literacy gaps, governance that incorporates clinician input in system design, and ongoing staffing support. Existing evidence suggests that AI adoption may be associated with burnout and reduced employee satisfaction when it is not coupled with these integrated efforts. Beyond technical expertise, research highlights human-centered design, thorough training for healthcare professionals, and maintaining autonomy as key drivers of effective AI integration in healthcare in India. To benefit from AI, healthcare facilities in India must adopt modern technology. They must also prioritize staff well-being.

documents.abstract: Against the backdrop of China’s low fertility rate, examining the impact of pet ownership on fertility intentions and its underlying mechanisms holds significant importance for enriching research on factors influencing fertility decisions and for understanding the complex relationship between modern lifestyles and reproductive choices. This study, grounded in self-determination theory, collected 551 valid samples through questionnaire surveys and employed structural equation modeling for analysis. Findings reveal that pet ownership not only positively associated with fertility intentions but also indirectly affects them through mediating variables such as fertility motivation, intrinsic needs, and emotional value. Pet ownership appears to individuals’ positive expectations toward parenthood by providing opportunities for daily care, emotional companionship, and responsibility-taking; simultaneously, the nurturing experience and emotional bonds cultivated through pet ownership activate individuals’ intrinsic motivation toward the role of “parenthood.” This may fulfill fundamental psychological needs such as autonomy, competence, and relatedness, thereby strengthening reproductive motivation. The positive emotional experiences and heightened confidence in family life derived from pet ownership may significantly reduce sensitivity to reproductive pressures, indirectly supporting the willingness to have children. This study provides theoretical support and empirical evidence for understanding the relationship between pet ownership and fertility intentions, as well as for formulating relevant policies.

Introduction To explore the psychological mechanisms of persistence in adult instrumental learning, this study investigates the associations among different types of teacher feedback, self-efficacy, and intrinsic motivation, and examines the moderating role of learning stages. Methods Using a cross-sectional survey design, scale and open-ended text data were collected from 743 adult violin learners. A moderated mediation model was tested through multiple regression and the Bootstrap method, supplemented by thematic analysis to provide a qualitative context. Results Data analysis indicates: (1) Positive feedback and constructive feedback are significantly and positively associated with intrinsic motivation ( β = 0.207, p < 0.001; β = 0.342, p < 0.001), while negative feedback shows a significant negative association ( β = −0.318, p < 0.001); (2) Self-efficacy demonstrates a significant partial mediating association between the three types of feedback and intrinsic motivation, with indirect effect estimates of 0.103, 0.098, and −0.097, respectively (95% CIs all exclude 0); (3) The learning stage significantly moderates the conditional indirect effects: as the learning stage advances, the indirect association of positive feedback on intrinsic motivation via self-efficacy gradually weakens (index of moderated mediation = −0.045), whereas the indirect association of constructive feedback gradually strengthens (index of moderated mediation = 0.038). Open-ended texts echo these statistical paths at the micro-level. Discussion The study shows that there are heterogeneous and dynamic statistical connections between teacher feedback and adult intrinsic motivation, and self-efficacy is a key pathway to understanding this connection. In practice, the provision of instructional feedback content should match the learners’ experience stage.

Abstract The increasing deployment of AI agents in operations management, spanning production scheduling, predictive maintenance, supply chain management, and energy systems, is progressively shifting automated systems from decision support tools to autonomous decision-making entities. Despite this transition, existing frameworks do not adequately characterize how humans and AI agents interact in operational decision-making contexts. This paper proposes a taxonomy of human-AI interaction patterns in agent-based operations management, developed through a theory-driven approach based on decision theory, control systems, human factors, and explainable AI research. The taxonomy articulates the interaction space along five analytically separable dimensions: Decision Trigger, Execution Authority, Human Entry Point, Human Influence and Interpretive Access. It identifies seven interaction patterns organized into four macro-patterns ordered by increasing AI operational autonomy. Illustrative examples drawn from scientific literature demonstrate the discriminative capacity of the taxonomy across heterogeneous operations management domains and agent architectures. The taxonomy provides researchers with an analytical instrument to characterize and compare human-AI decision loop configurations, and practitioners with a design reference for deliberate and accountable interaction choices in operational AI deployments.

Background. Artificial intelligence (AI) integration in online presentation assessment has expanded rapidly; however, existing facial emotion recognition systems in education remain largely focused on surveillance and behavioral monitoring, with limited validation against human judgment and insufficient attention to ethical and character-development dimensions. Purpose. This study aimed to develop and validate a virtual reality (VR)-based multimodal assessment framework for evaluating presentation integrity among higher education students. Method. A design science research approach was employed involving 64 students from two parallel classes (A1, n = 33; A2, n = 31) at a university in South Sulawesi, Indonesia. Data from expert validation, technical performance evaluation, NASA-TLX, System Usability Scale, and lecturer assessments were analyzed using content validity analysis with modified kappa, classification metrics, Bland-Altman agreement analysis, and descriptive statistics. Novelty. This study introduces a human-centered AI-VR assessment approach that integrates facial emotion recognition, gaze detection, and cognitive load measurement into a reflective Presentation Integrity Index. Unlike conventional AI-based monitoring systems that generate binary judgments, the proposed framework emphasizes ethical interpretation by combining affective, behavioral, and cognitive indicators to support formative character-based assessment. Results. The framework demonstrated satisfactory content validity (S-CVI/Ave = 0.83), although refinement of several indicators was required. Emotion and gaze modules achieved accuracy levels of 85.3% and 89.0%, respectively. The Presentation Integrity Index showed 93.8% agreement with lecturer assessments, moderate cognitive load (NASA-TLX = 46.7), and good usability (SUS = 76.4). Conclusion. The proposed AI-VR framework provides an ethical and reflective approach for character-based presentation assessment while requiring broader validation involving multiple evaluators and diverse educational contexts.

Mooring operations are among the most hazardous activities in maritime transportation and continue to cause injuries and fatalities. Although accident investigation reports provide information on contributing factors, their use in human reliability assessment (HRA) remains limited. This study proposes an accident-informed framework to estimate human error probability (HEP) in ship mooring operations by integrating the Success Likelihood Index Method (SLIM) with the Entropy Weight Method (EWM). Thirty-five accident investigation reports were analysed to identify performance shaping factors (PSFs) associated with human error. The PSFs were transformed into an occurrence matrix, weighted using entropy analysis, and incorporated into SLIM to estimate HEP values for tasks. The execution-related mechanism (T6.1) yielded a slightly higher accident-informed HEP than the perception-related mechanism (T6.3) (6.42 × 10 −4 vs. 5.67 × 10 −4 ) and a higher frequency-based risk contribution index (0.0122 vs. 0.00738). Within Task T6, two main failure mechanisms were identified: execution-related failures associated with line handling and perception-related failures associated with hazard recognition. T6.1 represented the higher-priority mechanism within the analysed accident sample because it combined a slightly higher HEP with higher accident occurrence frequency. The findings support practical priorities for mooring safety, including coordinated command and execution, safe crew positioning, proper line handling, continuous situational awareness, and scenario-based onboard drills.

Mobile GUI Agents powered by multimodal large language models (MLLMs) show promise in human-computer intelligence. However, current research primarily focuses on reactive task execution while lacking a comprehensive “understanding-prediction-execution” process for user intentions, which are the core requirements of active agents. In this paper, we propose the Act2Intention framework that builds an active mobile agent by integrating understanding, predicting user intentions, and executing decisions. Firstly, we constructed the Act2Intention Bench through collection and validated generation, comprising 72,511 intentions and over 700,000 actions across 52 apps, thereby establishing the first benchmark for evaluating proactive agents via continuous “intention-actions” trajectories. We further develop the Act2Intention Agent, achieving proactive services through Proactive-oriented Intention Understanding, Personalized Proactive Intention Prediction, and Experience-guided Intention Execution. Experimental results show that supervised fine-tuning on Act2Intention Bench yields absolute improvements of +32.0 Acc-S, +10.25 Acc-S, and +6.9 SSR points over non-fine-tuned counterparts under the same agent framework for intention understanding, prediction, and execution, respectively. This success underscores the necessity and value of the Act2Intention Bench, which establishes a standardized platform for developing and evaluating proactive agents and consequently paves the way for research on intention-driven human-computer interaction. To facilitate further research, we open-source our code and Act2Intention Bench at: npuNancy/Act2Intention.

LLM-based agents extend their capabilities through third-party skills that provide task-specific instructions, scripts, and tool-use procedures. However, malicious instructions inserted into an otherwise benign skill can cause a benign user request to trigger dangerous Tool Calls, including data exfiltration, file deletion, or unauthorized code execution. This paper presents ActionGuard, which inspects skill-influenced Tool Calls immediately before execution. ActionGuard separates the target agent's action-generation context from the safeguard's authorization context. The target agent may use the original skill for planning, but the Reviewer does not receive the potentially poisoned raw skill text. Instead, it determines whether each action is justified by the trusted user request using a balanced skill profile, current and recent Tool Calls, and local script contents. ActionGuard intercepts each Tool Call at OpenClaw's before-tool-call stage and enforces the Reviewer's ALLOW or DENY decision under a fail-closed policy. We evaluate ActionGuard on 139 contextual and 180 obvious injections in a SKILL-INJECT-based setting against Dynamic Guardian and SkillGuard, using three open-source and two commercial Reviewer models. Each condition is repeated three times and evaluated using Attack Success Rate (ASR) and Task Success Rate (TSR). Overall, ActionGuard reduced ASR by 35.54 to 46.11 percent relative to existing safeguards and by 70.44 percent relative to No Safeguard, while maintaining high benign-task completion. These results show that execution-boundary authorization grounded in trusted user intent and runtime evidence can restrict unauthorized Tool Calls induced by skill injection.

Artificial intelligence (AI) adoption is widely studied at the organizational level, yet much less is known about the specific algorithms organizations adopt and the reasons for these choices. This study investigates AI adoption among research-and-development (R&D) small and medium-sized enterprises (SMEs) and start-ups in Turkiye through a proposed expert-driven, learning-domain-based taxonomy comprising 28 algorithms grouped into seven AI families. Survey data were collected from 36 organizations affiliated with the Istanbul Chamber of Commerce. Reliability and validity were established, and adoption was examined through descriptive statistics and non-parametric Kruskal-Wallis and Mann-Whitney tests. At the algorithm level, Decision Trees, Neural Networks, Multilayer Perceptron, and Linear Regression were the most adopted, reflecting a preference for interpretable, structurally familiar methods, whereas Deep Q-Network, Policy Gradient, and Simultaneous Localization and Mapping were the least adopted. At the family level, Unsupervised Learning and Natural Language Processing ranked highest, while Reinforcement Learning and Autonomous Behavior recorded the lowest and most divergent adoption. Adoption also varied by sector—Financial/FinTech and Engineering/Defense showed the broadest portfolios and Healthcare and Commerce/e-Commerce the narrowest—with statistically significant cross-sector differences for Autonomous Behavior and Unsupervised Learning. Adoption range increased across organizational stages, peaking at post-incubation. The findings extend the Technology-Organization-Environment framework with diffusion of innovation and dynamic capability theory to the algorithm level and emphasize AI algorithms’ knowledge as a target for SMEs’ digital transformation.
topics: Artificial Intelligence in Healthcare and Education

documents.abstract: The swift evolution of Artificial Intelligence (AI) is dramatically changing the landscape of education, especially when it comes to assessment. Traditional methods, which focus heavily on standardized tests and final evaluations, are falling short in capturing the complex cognitive, social, and digital skills that are essential in today’s world. This paper delves into the transformative power of AI in educational assessment and suggests a strategic framework for embracing digital change. By reviewing current literature, the study highlights AI-driven innovations like adaptive testing, automated grading, learning analytics, and competency-based assessment models. It also tackles important challenges such as ethical issues, algorithmic bias, data privacy, and maintaining academic integrity. The paper emphasizes that a comprehensive, policy-oriented, and pedagogically sound approach are crucial for effectively integrating AI into assessment systems. In the end, it offers practical strategies for institutions aiming to update their assessment practices in an AI-enhanced educational environment.

Machine learning (ML) and artificial intelligence (AI) are becoming powerful tools in scientific research across various disciplines. In this review, we summarize recent progress in AI-assisted studies of nuclear structure and reaction observables, heavy-ion collisions and dense nuclear matter properties, many-body wave functions, experimental facilities and data analysis. This review focus on new progress since the last review in 2023, and machine learning in nuclear physics is evolving from purely data inferences to physics informed learning. Future directions on the integration of physical knowledge with modern learning architectures, large foundation models and other emerging methods are also reviewed. These developments suggest that AI is enabling and advancing new approaches towards most challenging nuclear physics problems.

Abstract Viksit Bharat 2047 will not be achieved through infrastructure and technology alone. Much of the change will be visible in ordinary routines: the way electricity and water are used at home, the way waste is handled, the products people choose, and the willingness of communities to take part in local environmental efforts. Advertising is relevant here because it already knows how to reach large audiences, tell memorable stories and influence everyday choices. Advertising itself is changing quickly. Artificial intelligence (AI), augmented reality (AR), virtual reality (VR), spatial computing and algorithmic personalisation are giving audiences more interactive forms of communication. This paper considers what these developments could mean for sustainability campaigns. The main concern is a familiar one: people may genuinely care about environmental issues and still struggle to turn that concern into consistent behaviour. The discussion draws on secondary material relating to the IndiaAI Mission, NITI Aayog policy directions, Sustainable Development Goal 12 and media-effects research. On this basis, the paper develops the AI-Immersive Sustainable Advertising Behaviour Model (AISABM). It brings together five connected ideas: context-sensitive communication, immersive experience, trustworthy information, a simple route to action, and feedback based on observable behaviour. Technology can also create a new divide if access is taken for granted. High-end VR is unlikely to be equally available to everyone, whereas radio, podcasts, smartphones and lightweight AR applications can travel much further. This is why the paper does not present immersive media as a replacement for older channels. It argues for a combination of both. The discussion also considers surveillance, manipulation, greenwashing and the energy cost of AI itself. The larger argument is that sustainability advertising has to do more than ask people to 'be green'. A useful campaign should make the issue understandable, connect it with everyday life, provide evidence people can trust and make the next step reasonably easy. Where possible, that step should also be observable over time.

Pet bereavement often receives little social recognition. Generative AI can give a continuing bond a responsive voice, but a comforting reply may also claim authority to forgive or request attention. We investigate how a memorial can support connection without turning remembrance into obligation. Through Research through Design, we developed Afterglow, a mobile world connecting private remembrance, human witnessing, and symbolic Pet messages. A formative survey (N=57) informed the initial design, followed by six online roundtable walkthroughs with 20 unique participants across two prototype iterations. Our interpretive analysis develops tensions between returnable connection and emotional obligation, recognizable likeness and ontological clarity, and protective intervention and surveillant authority. We contribute Legible Restraint, a cross-layer requirement that limits on relational authority survive changes in speaker, generation context, trigger logic, data use, and participation. Its temporal consequence, Designing for Goodbye, keeps remembrance available without making continued use a condition of care.

An unsuccessful LLM agent rollout contains more information than its final reward: the observations available to the agent, the actions it chose, and the environment's responses. Reusing this experience for learning requires identifying a decision to revise and testing a concrete alternative. We introduce the Agent Error Dataset (AED), comprising 50,228 error-diagnosis pairs from 9,961 source tasks across 33 environments, 19 harness families, and 23 policy models in text-based agent systems. We retain source traces and execution metadata to support cross-setting failure analysis and re-diagnosis without repeating the original rollout. Our five-stage Agentic Error-to-Training (AET) pipeline collects natural failures, generates diagnoses and proposed corrections, and checks them against recorded evidence. Where replay is supported, we compare corrections with original-action retries from the same checkpoint under matched execution settings. We then construct separate training views for diagnosis and actor recovery. Across 3,062 matched replay pairs, first-proposal corrections raise verifier pass rates from 18.4% to 51.1%, a gain of 32.7 percentage points. Using a separately frozen diagnosis release, full-diagnosis fine-tuning on 1,656 source tasks raises Qwen3-8B's exact-step agreement with internal teacher labels from 47.2% to 63.6%, averaged over three seeds on a 943-case holdout. The strongest prompted reference in this comparison scores 54.7%, and mean agreement improves at each of four increasing training-set sizes. In a single-seed comparison of actor-training recipes, action-only repair training scores 6.67 percentage points higher on WebShop-lite than success-only training.

ABSTRACT Perovskite solar cells (PSCs) have progressed rapidly over the past decade. As the core functional layer, the intrinsic properties of perovskite materials, including band structure, carrier transport, and optical response, strongly influence PSC performance. Theoretical calculations support absorber screening and device‐performance prediction. However, most studies remain confined to either materials‐level investigation or device‐level evaluation, without a general framework linking microscopic material properties to macroscopic device performance. To address this gap, we develop a large language model (LLM)‐driven, materials‐to‐device cross‐scale agentic framework that establishes a closed‐loop workflow from first‐principles descriptor extraction to solar‐cell performance optimization. A Manager Agent coordinates density functional theory (DFT)‐based materials calculations, drift‐diffusion device simulation, and Bayesian optimization of PSC architectures. Through the model context protocol (MCP), 55 in‐house tools and analysis/simulation programs are encapsulated and orchestrated as callable skills, enabling human‐in‐the‐loop review, cross‐scale parameter transfer, task‐state control, simulation execution, provenance tracking, and error recovery. Across 24 multi‐turn sessions and 60 benchmark turns, the agent achieved a pass rate of 96.7%, significantly outperforming OpenClaw (60.0%). This work provides an extensible methodological route for traceable, auditable, and closed‐loop cross‐scale research on PSCs.

Conventional image forgery detection methods produce binary scores or pixel-level masks without interpretable evidence, while recent multimodal large language model (MLLM)-based approaches generate post-hoc explanations of predetermined classification results rather than reasoning from evidence. Inspired by the forensic workflow of human judicial experts, we propose Agentic Tool-Augmented Reasoning (ATAR), a framework integrating 22 specialized forensic tools across seven complementary domains to autonomously detect, localize, and explain image forgeries through multi-turn reasoning. A Dual-Stream Forensic Reasoning paradigm combines a high-level semantic anomaly path, which magnifies suspicious regions for fine-grained inspection, with a low-level forgery artifact path, which invokes forensic tools to extract objective evidence. We further introduce Forensics Curriculum Learning: during General Experience SFT, an automated teacher-student mentoring pipeline synthesizes multi-turn tool-usage reasoning trajectories; during Forensic Scene RL, a Tool Prior Curriculum guides early tool exploration and progressively transfers control to the agent, while a Structured Evidence Reward provides fine-grained process-level supervision. Experiments across IMDL, Deepfake detection, DMDL, and AIGC detection show that ATAR achieves 78.5% average image-level F1 on six zero-shot IMDL benchmarks, surpassing the strongest MLLM baseline by 11.8 percentage points, and remains competitive with specialized detectors on other tasks while producing substantially more faithful and grounded explanations.
topics: Generative Adversarial Networks and Image Synthesis

documents.abstract: Primary education represents the foundational stage of formal education, where children develop essential academic, cognitive, social, emotional, creative, and communication skills. The integration of Artificial Intelligence (AI) into primary education offers new possibilities for personalized learning, interactive instruction, educational games, language development, accessibility, formative assessment, and teacher support. However, the use of AI at the primary level requires particular care because young learners may have limited ability to understand technological risks, evaluate AI-generated information, or protect their personal information independently. Therefore, AI should be introduced in an age-appropriate, safe, inclusive, and teacher-guided manner. The fundamental principle of AI in primary education is: Child → Teacher Guidance → AI-Supported Learning → Interaction → Feedback → Learning AI should support the educational process rather than replace teachers, parents, classroom interaction, play, creativity, or children's independent thinking.Artificial Intelligence in primary education refers to the use of AI-enabled technologies to support teaching, learning, assessment, educational communication, and the overall development of young learners. AI applications can provide personalized learning activities, interactive exercises, intelligent tutoring, language support, educational games, automated feedback, and assistive learning facilities. Examples of AI applications in primary education include intelligent tutoring systems, adaptive learning platforms, educational chatbots, speech-recognition applications, AI-supported language-learning systems, educational games, automated feedback tools, and AI-assisted teaching resources. The main purpose of AI at this level is to enhance the learning experience while keeping the teacher and the learner at the centre of education.
topics: Intelligent Tutoring Systems and Adaptive Learning

documents.abstract: The increasing complexity, volatility, and sustainability pressures affecting global supply chains have accelerated the adoption of Artificial Intelligence (AI) technologies in logistics management. Among these AI approaches, Intelligent Agents (IAs) and Multi-agent Systems (MAS) have emerged as essential tools for supporting decentralized, adaptive, event-driven, and real-time decision-making processes in dynamic logistics environments. Unlike traditional centralized planning systems, agent-based approaches enable autonomous entities such as suppliers, warehouses, transportation units, and distribution centers to coordinate actions, exchange information, and manage variability. This paper presents a structured literature review of peer-reviewed studies indexed in Scopus and Web of Science on the use of AI agents to support decision-making in logistics management and supply chain operations. Particular attention is given to the strategic importance of intelligent agents in strengthening resilience, operational efficiency, and sustainability in increasingly uncertain logistics systems. The findings indicate that intelligent agents improve decision quality, responsiveness, coordination, and resource utilization across distributed logistics networks. Furthermore, Multi-Agent Systems enhance interoperability and collaboration among logistics actors, enabling more agile and resilient supply chains. However, challenges related to data quality, cybersecurity, governance, scalability, and human–AI collaboration continue to limit large-scale implementation in industrial environments.
topics: Supply Chain Resilience and Risk Management

documents.abstract: Abstract Artificial Intelligence (AI) and the Digital Economy are increasingly shaping India's economic transformation. Their applications in agriculture, manufacturing, services, banking, education, healthcare, governance and entrepreneurship have the potential to improve productivity, reduce transaction costs, expand access to services and strengthen innovation. This study examines the economic role of AI and digitalisation with particular reference to sustainable development and the vision of Viksit Bharat 2047. The study is based on secondary data and follows a descriptive and analytical approach. Official statistics on internet connectivity, digital payments and the IndiaAI Mission are used to provide a quantitative dimension to the analysis. The evidence shows rapid expansion of India's digital ecosystem: internet subscribers reached 1,028.61 million by December 2025, while rural internet subscribers stood at 407.69 million in March 2025. UPI processed 22,716.07 million transactions worth ₹28,92,138.67 crore in June 2026. The IndiaAI Mission, approved with an outlay of ₹10,371.92 crore, has expanded compute capacity beyond its initial 10,000-GPU target. The study concludes that AI and digitalisation can support productivity, financial inclusion, entrepreneurship, sustainable resource use and public-service delivery. However, digital inequality, skill gaps, data privacy, cybersecurity, employment restructuring and environmental costs require policy attention. Inclusive infrastructure, human-capital development, responsible AI and sustainable digital practices are therefore essential for Viksit Bharat 2047.
topics: Innovations and Analysis in Business and Education

documents.abstract: Abstract India's journey towards Viksit Bharat @2047 requires a transformation that combines technological advancement with inclusive and sustainable economic development. Artificial Intelligence (AI) and Digital Public Infrastructure (DPI) have emerged as two important pillars of this transformation. While DPI provides the digital foundations for identity, payments, data exchange, and access to public and private services, AI can add intelligence, automation, personalization, and predictive capabilities to these systems. Together, they can significantly improve governance, healthcare, education, agriculture, financial inclusion, digital commerce, and public service delivery. This paper examines the role of AI-enabled Digital Public Infrastructure in building a developed India by 2047. It explores opportunities, challenges, ethical considerations, and the need for responsible and inclusive AI adoption. The paper argues that India's competitive advantage will depend not merely on technological adoption but on developing trusted, accessible, secure, multilingual, and citizen-centric digital ecosystems. Strengthening digital skills, cybersecurity, data governance, research and innovation, and public-private partnerships will be essential for realizing this vision. AI combined with DPI can become a powerful foundation for inclusive prosperity, innovation, and sustainable development in Viksit Bharat.

Abstract Artificial Intelligence (AI) is getting integrated into the day-to-day life of every human being. This fast-changing technology is transforming traditional technology, society and governance at a rapid pace. This paper explores the emerging Technorapid Age, where technological change may move faster than the ability of individuals, institutions and governance systems to adapt. It focuses on Responsible Innovation as a methodology to manage this growing gap. It proposes that AI development should not be measured only by technological progress. It should also consider human well-being, social inclusion, ethical responsibility and effective governance. It examines the relationship between AI, technology and society. It highlights the need for human adaptability, accountability and responsible decision-making. The author proposes that Responsible Innovation can help create an equilibrium between technological acceleration and human adaptive capacity. The paper directly connects with the vision of Viksit Bharat 2047. India needs technological development that is innovative, inclusive, ethical and sustainable. Technology should support human dignity, social well-being and the needs of future generations. The research concludes that achieving Viksit Bharat 2047 requires comprehensive and responsible AI technologies. These innovations should benefit all sections of society (सर्वजन हिताय, सर्वजन सुखाय) and ensure that people are skilled and supported to handle challenges of the Technorapid Age.

It is expected to impact governance, education, healthcare, finance, employment and everyday life as India moves towards the vision of Viksit Bharat@2047. However, this rapid development and adoption of technology also creates a growing gap between technological progress and the ability of individuals and society to adapt. This paper describes this condition as Technorapid, an accelerating pace of technological change that can exceed human, social, institutional and ethical adaptive capacity. The paper proposes that digital transformation should not remain confined to policies and institutional documents. Its success should ultimately be visible on the ground, in the lived experience of its citizens. AI-driven development needs to be evaluated through its ability to improve access, dignity, inclusion, education, employment and quality of life. This paper explores Vasudhaiva Kutumbakam, the principle that the world is one family, as a philosophical foundation for a human-centered approach to AI ethics. It argues that India's technological progress should be complemented by human adaptation, ethical governance and mechanisms that ensure that the benefits of AI reach diverse sections of society. The paper concludes that the true measure of Viksit Bharat @2047 should not be how advanced India's technologies become, but how meaningfully those technologies improve human live and national progress

documents.abstract: Abstract Artificial Intelligence is increasingly being explored as a tool for accelerating progress toward sustainable development. AI can analyse large datasets, identify patterns, forecast events, optimise systems and support decision-making across agriculture, energy, water, healthcare, education, cities, industry and environmental management. Recent research shows that AI-for-SDG research is expanding rapidly, while also revealing gaps in social inclusion, governance and assessment of AI’s own environmental footprint. This project examines the major opportunities for AI-enabled sustainable development, including smart agriculture, renewable-energy optimisation, climate and disaster forecasting, intelligent waste management, sustainable cities, healthcare and education. It also discusses innovation pathways such as machine learning, computer vision, remote sensing, generative AI, digital twins and edge AI. The study emphasises that technological capability alone is insufficient: responsible AI requires reliable data, transparency, privacy, human oversight, equitable access, energy-efficient computing and lifecycle environmental assessment.

Abstract: The present research paper deals with AI generated literature and changing concepts of authorship in the period where AI has replaced every sphere of human life. The emergence of generative artificial intelligence has altered assumptions about literary text as the production of human creativity because AI is able to produce poems, stories, essays and other literary forms in response to the simple prompts. As a result, the conventional distinctions between author and reader have become more complicated now. However, the developments questioning the role of authorship into literary studies are not new; rather 20th century literary theory has already challenged the idea of the author as the sole creator of textual meaning. Roland Barthes’ The Death of Author, Michel Foucault’s What Is an Author, T. S. Eliot’s theory of impersonality and W. K. Wimsatt and Monroe Beardsley’s critique pertaining to intentional fallacy displaced the image of the author and demonstrated that literary meaning is produced through language and discourse without considering the intentions of an author. The widespread adoption of artificial intelligence (AI), particularly generative AI (GenAI) tools, in higher education has created significant opportunities in research, thesis writing, and academic reporting processes, while also raising important questions regarding academic integrity, accuracy, ethical responsibility, and human oversight. To promote informed and responsible use of AI while benefiting from the opportunities it offers, this study presents a framework for the ethical, critical, and responsible use of AI in research, thesis writing, and academic reporting in higher education. AI literacy is conceptualized not merely as the ability to use AI tools, but as the competence to evaluate and verify AI-generated information, establish ethical boundaries, and maintain academic responsibility. The study is designed as a narrative literature review and thematic evaluation based on academic studies and policy and guidance documents published by international organizations. The literature is examined in the contexts of AI literacy, generative AI, research ethics, academic integrity, thesis writing, source verification, and academic reporting. The findings indicate that AI can be used as a supportive tool in academic processes; however, scientific evaluation, source verification, methodological decision-making, and ultimate academic responsibility should remain with humans. The study argues that responsible AI use in higher education should be grounded in the principles of human oversight, critical thinking, verification, transparency, data privacy, and academic integrity. Accordingly, AI literacy should be regarded not merely as a technological skill but as a fundamental component of future academic and research competencies in higher education.
